name: Cross Collar Choke from Invisible Collar
summary: The Cross Collar Choke uses crossed grips in the opponent's jacket collar so the forearms and tightened cloth close space on both sides of the neck.
description: Cross Collar Choke from Invisible Collar requires jacket grips. Establish crossed collar connections separately from the high rubber-guard leg clinch.
target_area: Sides of the neck via crossed forearms and collar tension
overview:
The attacker faces the opponent with access to both jacket collars and enough posture control to establish the grips. Invisible Collar names a high leg clinch, not a cloth grip. Releasing that clinch and arranging actual collar access is necessary; the reviewed primary lesson demonstrates mount rather than a direct Invisible Collar entry.

Keep the opponent close enough to reach the collar without extending both arms unsupported. Take a secure collar grip beside the neck rather than a shallow handful of cloth. Bring the second hand to the opposite collar using the grip orientation taught for the chosen variation. Place the forearms beside the neck without dragging across the jaw or bending the wrists painfully.

The collar must be used as a controlled choking surface, never to grind the face. Release both grips promptly and do not test how long a partner can tolerate the choke.

Instructional sources: [Stephan Kesting and Rob Biernacki — cross-collar choke](https://www.grapplearts.com/cross-collar-choke-mount/); [Eddie Bravo — MTS 134 Invisible Collar in Austin](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KCyIwacRKu8).

flashcards.question: Cross-collar practice: why does a shallow first grip demand more pulling later?
flashcards.answer: Loose cloth leaves extra space beside the neck. A shallow handful of cloth can leave slack between the collar and the neck. Establish a supported grip and check its placement without finishing pressure, rather than compensating with a sudden pull.

trap: Pulling the jaw replaces the need to remove collar slack

A leg pummel that keeps the top player centered

flashcards.question: Cross-collar defense: how many grips are complete when you first contest the entering hand?
flashcards.answer: Neither grip is complete; contest the first entering hand. Stop it gaining depth before the second hand crosses. Early hand fighting is preferable to treating two secured collar grips as the starting point.
flashcards.answer_line: Neither grip is complete; contest the first entering hand

plausible: Both hands have already crossed and tightened
The second hand is deep while the first remains outside
trap: Both wrists are fixed against the neck under pressure

flashcards.answer: The second hand crossing to the opposite collar. Keep an inside frame before the hands cross into a complete choke.
flashcards.answer_line: The second hand crossing to the opposite collar

plausible: All movement of the opponent's far ankle
Your own shoulder returning toward the neck
trap: The attacker's free knee moving on the mat

flashcards.question: Cross-collar defense: before any cloth grip is caught, what distance can posture preserve?
flashcards.answer: Distance between your neck and the reaching hands. Use posture and distance while the jacket connections are still available to deny. Once the neck is secured, do not try to force posture against a loaded choke.
flashcards.answer_line: Distance between your neck and the reaching hands

plausible: A gap between your own knees while the neck stays captured
More slack at the belt without changing the upper body
trap: Space behind the attacker's heels only

flashcards.question: Cross-collar defense: what must you create in the cloth enclosure before a larger body escape?
flashcards.answer: Slack between the collar restraint and your neck. Address the grips while space remains so body movement is not made against a fixed neck restraint. A secured choke calls for an early tap.

plausible: A tighter crossing of the attacker's wrists
A lower chin without changing either cloth grip
trap: A sideways head angle inside the same tight collar loop
